# Moggallāna Saṁyutta (SN 40)
**ID:** SN 40
**Section:** Saṁyuttanikāya (sn)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Moggallāna Saṁyutta* (SN 40) is the fortieth collection of the *Saṁyuttanikāya*, comprising eleven discourses centered on Mahāmoggallāna, one of the Buddha's two chief disciples [SuttaCentral; Bhikkhu Bodhi 2003]. In the first nine suttas, Moggallāna recounts his meditative struggles prior to enlightenment, which spanned the progressive stages of absorption: the four *jhāna*s, the four formless attainments (*arūpajjhāna*: the base of infinite space, infinite consciousness, nothingness, and neither-perception-nor-nonperception), and the signless concentration of mind (*animitta cetosamādhi*) [Bhikkhu Bodhi 2003; Hazra 1994; Nyanaponika, Hecker, and Bodhi 2003]. At each meditative hurdle—beginning in the first *jhāna*, where sensory perceptions and distracting thoughts arose—Moggallāna was assisted by the Buddha, who intervened through psychic powers to offer guidance, admonishing him to steady, concentrate, and unify his mind (*cittam ekodiṃ karohi*) [Bhikkhu Bodhi 2003; Shankman 2008; Eifring 2014; Hung 2010]. In the commentary (*Sāratthappakāsinī*), this signless concentration of mind is identified with insight concentration (*vipassanāsamādhi*) [Miracapillo n.d.]. In the final two discourses, Moggallāna travels to heavenly realms to preach to deities such as Sakka on taking refuge in the Triple Gem [SuttaCentral; Bhikkhu Bodhi 2003].
Curated parallels in the Chinese *Saṁyuktāgama* (T 99) correspond to individual discourses, notably SĀ 502 for the *Animittapañhāsutta* (SN 40.9) and SĀ 506 and SĀ 988–989 for the *Sakkasutta* (SN 40.10) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus corroborates cross-language reuse with T 99 (fascicle 30), alongside alignments with the *Madhyama-āgama* (T 26) and Sanskrit Buddhist texts including the *Mahāvyutpatti*, *Arthaviniścayasūtra* (and its *Nibandhana*), *Avadānaśataka*, and *Divyāvadāna*, as well as Tibetan *Prajñāpāramitā* literature [DharmaNexus]. Within Pali canonical literature, DharmaNexus records extensive textual reuse between SN 40 and the *Sotāpatti Saṁyutta* (SN 55, with over 1,100 matching segments, especially around SN 40.10), various chapters of the *Aṅguttaranikāya* (AN 3, 4, 5, 8, 9, 10), the *Bhikkhu Saṁyutta* (SN 21), and multiple commentarial works [DharmaNexus].
